quote: there is no physical law precluding particles from being organized in ways that perform even more advanced computations than the arrangements of particles in human brains. An explosive transition is possible, although it may play out differently than in the movie: as Irving Good realized in 1965, machines with superhuman intelligence could repeatedly improve their design even further
claim_summary: Co-written piece: no physical law rules out machines that compute better than human brains, and an explosive transition to superhuman intelligence is possible.
definition_note: machines whose computations exceed those of human brains; 'superhuman intelligence'
notes: basis: "An explosive transition is possible"; Co-written opinion piece by Stephen Hawking, Stuart Russell, Max Tegmark and Frank Wilczek, 'Transcending Complacency on Superintelligent Machines', HuffPost contributor platform, byline date 2014-04-19 on the page; Russell is a named author (A14 ruling 3). Republished in The Independent 2014-05-01 (same text, not a separate row). Read at HuffPost (fetched with curl). The same piece also says 'If a superior alien civilization sent us a text message saying, "We'll arrive in a few decades," would we just reply, "OK, call us when you get here"... this is more or less what is happening with AI' - an analogy that hints at a few decades but is put in the aliens' mouth, so it is not coded as a timeline; judgment call, listed in the report. Endorsement: 'no physical law precluding' says it can be done, and 'is possible' is a hedge, not a statement that it will happen, so uncertain rather than accepts.

quote: To me, it seems inevitable that the capabilities of intelligent machines will increase not just because of physics but because we're starting to understand better and better how to get those machines to behave intelligently. So it wouldn't surprise me if it happened in my lifetime and I could easily imagine it happening in the lifetime of my children.
claim_summary: Asked how worried he is, says growing machine capability is inevitable and it would not surprise him if machines beyond human control arrived in his lifetime, or easily in his children's.
timeline_text: it wouldn't surprise me if it happened in my lifetime and I could easily imagine it happening in the lifetime of my children
definition_note: systems 'more intelligent than a human being', 'far more intelligent than the human race put together', earlier in the interview
notes: basis: "it wouldn't surprise me if it happened in my lifetime"; Transcript of CBC Radio Spark interview by Nora Young, hosted on Russell's own Berkeley page; broadcast date 2014-05-31 from his media list and the file name (PDF created 2014-06-01). Read in full. Ambiguous: target_capability, since "it" refers back to systems more intelligent than humans getting beyond our control, not a named capability; coded superintelligence. Endorsement uncertain: "wouldn't surprise me" and "could easily imagine" are hedges, not a prediction. Agency from his next sentence in the same answer ("the sooner we start solving this problem, the better"), outside the stored quote, so the governance frame rests on context. Same interview: five years ago most AI people would have said human-level AI was "Decades and decades or centuries away", "but now I think it seems as if it's a little bit closer"; and he explains an intelligence explosion as a system at human level that "can redesign itself using better hardware and better algorithms".

quote: Thus, the gap between authoritative statements of technological impossibility and the "miracle of understanding" (to borrow a phrase from Nathan Myhrvold) that renders the impossible possible may sometimes be measured not in centuries, as Rod Brooks suggests, but in hours.
claim_summary: Replying to Rodney Brooks, argues from the history of nuclear fission that confident claims that highly capable AI is centuries away can be overturned very fast.
timeline_text: may sometimes be measured not in centuries ... but in hours
definition_note: 'a highly capable decision maker' that 'can have an irreversible impact on humanity'; no named capability
notes: basis: "may sometimes be measured not in centuries"; Russell's contribution "Of Myths And Moonshine" to the Edge Reality Club conversation "The Myth of AI" (Jaron Lanier, conversation dated 11.14.14 on the page). Russell's reply is not dated on the page, so year precision only. Read in full at edge.org (fetched with curl). Mentions Rodney Brooks (a panel member) only as the target of the reply. Ambiguous: target_capability (the reply is about AI that could be "the end of the world", not a named level of capability). Endorsement uncertain: "may" with a general timing claim, and he says "None of this proves that AI ... will be the end of the world". Same piece: "AI research has been accelerating rapidly" and senior researchers are more optimistic than a few years ago.

quote: But if that problem is solved — and it's certainly not impossible — then we would see another big increase in machine capabilities. There are two or three problems like that where if all of those were solved, then it's not clear to me that there would be any major obstacle between there and human-level AI.
claim_summary: Says current systems lack abstract, hierarchical planning; if two or three such problems were solved he sees no clear major obstacle to human-level AI.
notes: basis: "if all of those were solved, then it's not clear to me that there would be any major obstacle"; Quanta Magazine Q&A by Natalie Wolchover, "Concerns of an Artificial Intelligence Pioneer", dated April 21, 2015 on the page; read in full (fetched with curl). Reprinted by Wired 2015-05-23 (same text, not a separate row). present_capability disputed: just before, he says hierarchical decision making is "one of the missing pieces right now". Same interview: success "would be an enormous thing. 'The biggest event in human history'", earlier "Probably it was just too far away", and he explains the intelligence explosion as machines that "will be able to work on AI just like we do and improve their own capabilities" (he is describing the idea, not endorsing it).

claim_summary: In a Cambridge talk, said (as reported) that AGI is not imminent, that he would not give a date because breakthroughs cannot be predicted, but that it might not be many decades away.

definition_note: AGI: 'a machine with human-level cognitive abilities' (the blogger's gloss)
notes: secondhand; basis: "they might not be many decades away"; Calum Chace's blog report (post dated May 16, 2015) of Russell's public lecture "The Long-Term Future of (Artificial) Intelligence" at the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, Cambridge, on 15 May 2015 (date in the post and in Russell's own media list). The words are the blogger's paraphrase, not a direct quotation; a video of the talk exists (YouTube) but has no transcript, so not checked. quote: “If we had computers a trillion times faster we wouldn’t have human-level AI; half in jest, one might say we’d just get wrong answers a trillion times sooner,” he says. “What matters are real conceptual and algorithmic breakthroughs, which are very hard to predict.”
claim_summary: Says faster computers alone would not give human-level AI; it needs conceptual and algorithmic breakthroughs, which are very hard to predict.
timeline_text: breakthroughs, which are very hard to predict
notes: Nature news feature by Declan Butler, "A world where everyone has a robot: why 2040 could blow your mind", published 24 February 2016 (date on nature.com); the reporter spoke to Russell, so elicitation interview, primary. nature.com now paywalls the piece; read at the Wayback Machine copy of the free 2016 news page (fetched with curl). Endorsement unexpressed: he rejects a route (raw computing speed) and says the breakthroughs are hard to predict, but does not say whether human-level AI will come (A15 ruling 4).

claim_summary: Says superintelligent machines will probably arrive in decades rather than sooner, giving time to plan, and that the safety problem looks feasible but not easy.
timeline_text: There are probably decades to plan for the arrival
notes: basis: "There are probably decades to plan for the arrival of superintelligent machines"; Russell's article "Should we fear supersmart robots?", Scientific American vol. 314, pp. 58-59, June 2016 issue (citation from his own page); read in the copy hosted on his Berkeley site (PDF read as text through r.jina.ai). The PDF breaks "researchers" across a line with a hyphen; joined here. A14 ruling 11: decades away is accepts; "probably" is not one of the hedges (may, might, could) that make a date uncertain. Agency from "Solving the safety problem ... seems to be feasible". Same article: "Still others think that superintelligent AI will never happen", answered with the Rutherford and Szilard story, which argues against "never".

notes: Russell's essay "Provably Beneficial Artificial Intelligence", in The Next Step: Exponential Life (BBVA OpenMind, 2017; citation from his own page; PDF metadata 2017-09-14), read in the copy on his Berkeley site through r.jina.ai. The text extraction splits the "ffi" letter group ("di ffi culty"); joined here. Ambiguous: endorsement. Same essay, answering the objection "Human-level AI is impossible": the claim "represents a foolhardy bet against human ingenuity"; and "The relevant timescale for human-level AI is less predictable, but of course that means it, like nuclear fission, might arrive considerably sooner than expected."

Before It Stops Us", 2019-10-08 (date in the URL and his own media list); nytimes.com refused automated fetching (403), read at the Wayback Machine 2019 copy. quote: It’s true that we are several breakthroughs away from human-level AI. But let’s not forget that these breakthroughs can happen overnight.

timeline_text: several breakthroughs away ... these breakthroughs can happen overnight
definition_note: human-level AI; he lists four missing capabilities (real language understanding, managing its own computation, cumulative learning, long-horizon reasoning and planning)
notes: basis: "these breakthroughs can happen overnight"; getAbstract journal interview by Michael Wiederstein, dated November 6, 2019 on the page; read in full (fetched with curl). Endorsement uncertain: "can" is a hedge on timing and he does not say when it will arrive.
